title: The Way We Don’t Live Now
gist: A Hedgehog Review essay argues Anthony Trollope deserves reading precisely because his charitable, forbearing view of people runs against a contemporary culture of hard opinions, partisanship and atomization. It contrasts his tempered judgment of flawed characters and political opponents with Austen and Dickens, and with today's 'circular firing squads' of American democracy.

themes.theme: Polarization and the cost of judgmental culture

insights.claim: Contemporary society is lonelier and more atomized than Trollope would have thought possible, and one cause may be a culture that prioritizes hard, fast opinions, rewards partisanship and pushes people into silos.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Frames social atomization and partisanship as cultural, not only economic, phenomena — relevant to reading persistent political polarization as a structural feature of the operating environment.
insights.quote: Ours is a lonelier, more atomized society than Trollope would have thought possible
insights.locator: This is not to say that

insights.claim: Modern culture incites each individual to act as a 'hanging judge', observing behavior and pronouncing indictments of character rather than tempering judgment with understanding.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Signals the author's view that outrage-driven discourse norms are corrosive to social cohesion.
insights.quote: Each of us is incited to be a hanging judge
insights.locator: This is not to say that

insights.claim: The idea that party lines and ideological purity are no sure guide to human decency now seems almost like arcane knowledge given the 'interlinked, circular firing squads' of contemporary American democracy.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: A pessimistic read on US political fragmentation: intra- and inter-party hostility is portrayed as the default state.
insights.quote: the network of interlinked, circular firing squads that make up American democracy today
insights.locator: Trollope understands that people have reasons

insights.claim: Deep-seated beliefs are rarely displaced by argument; following Swift, people hold foundational assumptions acquired pre-rationally, so changing them requires getting to know the person over a long, delicate process rather than debating.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Implies persuasion campaigns built on argument alone will underperform; belief change is slow and relational, which bears on expectations for political or social opinion shifts.
insights.quote: reasoning will never make a man correct an ill opinion, which by reasoning he never acquired
insights.locator: In “A Letter to a Young Clergyman,”

insights.claim: The case for reading Trollope rests on his being untimely: his genial, charitable attitude toward people runs counter to current mores rather than anticipating them.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Positions cultural value in counter-cyclical perspectives rather than 'relevance'.
insights.quote: The case for him begins by recognizing he should be read because he is not of our time.
insights.locator: Trollope’s perch within the canon is assured

insights.claim: Trollope's implicit strategy for social harmony: don't expect too much from others, be grateful for what good there is, strive to understand them, and laugh at them and then at yourself.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: A compact behavioral prescription for de-escalating social conflict.
insights.quote: Don’t expect too much from others; be grateful for what good there is; strive to understand them; laugh at them and then laugh at yourself.
insights.locator: Character, in several senses of the word

insights.claim: Trollope's fiction advocates a forbearance that is neither blind approval nor chilly tolerance, insisting indignation be leavened with compassion, curiosity and humility about one's own vices.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Offers a model of practical rather than idealistic social harmony as an alternative to purity-driven politics.
insights.quote: a forbearance that is neither blind approbation nor chilly tolerance

insights.claim: Unlike Austen, who uses psychological insight to mock and expose characters, Trollope provokes and then attenuates the reader's censure, always supplying a brief for the defense.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Illustrates two distinct modes of social judgment — exposure versus mitigation.
insights.locator: Small wonder that such a man

insights.claim: Trollope's villains are rarely cruel; their callousness is thoughtless rather than calculated, and he holds that wickedness, such as Crosbie's jilting of Lily Dale for money and status, is its own worst punishment.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Reflects a moral worldview in which weakness, not malice, drives most wrongdoing.

insights.claim: Trollope, a self-described 'advanced, but still a Conservative-Liberal', backed reforms such as better treatment of Irish Catholics and education for the poor while remaining suspicious of reforming zeal.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: A template for moderate, incrementalist politics skeptical of zeal on either side.
insights.quote: an advanced, but still a Conservative-Liberal

insights.claim: Trollope ran for a Commons seat as a Liberal in 1868 and was disgusted by the corruption and special pleading of electioneering, yet kept that cynicism fenced within broad respect for the Westminster system.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Shows institutional respect can coexist with cynicism about electoral practice.

insights.claim: Trollope portrays even reactionary Tories who opposed Catholic emancipation, franchise expansion and Corn Law repeal as endearing and sometimes noble, writing that the well-educated Conservative is 'generally the pleasantest man to be met'.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Example of cross-partisan charity the author sees as missing from current politics.
insights.quote: He who said that all Conservatives are stupid did not know them.
insights.locator: Trollope understands that people have reasons

insights.claim: Compared with Dickens, who uses aristocratic obsession with 'Blood' as an object of contempt, Trollope treats Thorne's pedigree fixation as a decent man's venial eccentricity.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Contrasts contempt-based and sympathy-based treatment of ideological opponents.
insights.locator: The tone is ironic but not sardonic.

insights.claim: Trollope's sketch of Mrs. Roper, a London boarding-house keeper losing respectable tenants, comments on the precarious state of the Victorian lower middle class and insists such people have interior lives beyond socioeconomic categories.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: A reminder that downward mobility in the lower middle class is experienced as loss of standing, not just income.
insights.quote: she has an interior life, and even passersby might intuit a little of it
insights.locator: The sheer gratuitousness of the passage

insights.claim: No male author since Shakespeare, or perhaps Richardson, showed as much interest as Trollope in portraying women as complex people, and his female characters are generally more admirable than the men around them.
insights.speaker: Hedgehog Review
insights.so_what: Literary-historical claim; limited direct market relevance.
insights.locator: A novelist knows things about his characters
